newsitem.title: GERMANY: Russian, German ministers spend Easter together.
newsitem.headline: Russian, German ministers spend Easter together.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov went to Easter mass with his German counterpart on Sunday as part of a relaxed visit combining both business and pleasure which would have been unthinkable just a few years ago.
Primakov and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel attended the church service in the small western town of Kierdich and then moved on to a wine-tasting session nearby.
The main purpose of the Russian minister's visit was to brief Germany on the results of the Helsinki superpower summit.
But, at his host's invitation, Primakov and his wife stayed on after Saturday morning's formal talks to spend the rest of the weekend in the company of the Kinkels.
Primakov repaid the compliment by refusing to dwell on Russia's failure to hold up NATO enlargement and instead insisting Moscow need not suffer many disadvantages.

Primakov's trip, three weeks before a visit by President Boris Yeltsin, was recognition of the growing role Russia's one-time foe now plays in getting the West's point of view across to Russia and in helping Russia integrate with the West.

Bonn has insisted strongly on the need to respect Moscow's security interests in a planned NATO-Russia charter to be agreed as NATO prepares to ignore virulent Russian objections by inviting eastern European countries to join.
In Bonn, Primakov praised Kinkel and Chancellor Helmut Kohl for the ideas they had put forward.

He insisted the charter could answer criticism from the communist-led parliament at home that Yeltsin sold out Russian security interests to U.S. President Bill Clinton at their Helsinki summit 10 days ago.

"If we succeed in signing a document of substance that defines our relationship with NATO, we will try to neutralise to the maximum extent, to the maximum possible, the consequences of NATO enlargement for our relations with the West," he told a news conference after talks with Kinkel.
But he said intensive work still had to be done on the charter to counter Russian concerns "that NATO infrastructure will roll towards our borders".
It was "very important" for Russia that Clinton had reiterated to Yeltsin that NATO had no plans in the foreseeable future to deploy troops in eastern Europe, Primakov said.
The relaxed nature of the visit betrayed a sense of optimism and good relations a world away from the frosty climate which characterised ties between Bonn and Moscow during the Cold War.
The ministers appeared to be getting along well, smiling and laughing as they toured Kloster Eberbach, a monastery perched above the Rhine, before sampling some of the local wine.

The warm climate between two men was also apparent at Saturday's news conference when they discussed the subject of cultural treasures victorious Soviet troops took from Germany at the end of World War Two, and which Bonn would like back.

Kinkel spoke appreciatively of a decision by Yeltsin to block a Russian parliamentary bill which would have ruled out any return of the treasures and then went on to personally welcome Primakov's wife.
The often-dour Primakov laughed and quickly added: "I take it from the comments of Minister Kinkel that he sees my wife's visit as part of the transfer of cultural goods to Germany."
